abstract: |
 \agentformat{For a Data Descriptor, revise the abstract sentence reporting higher same-source correlations and decreasing variability so it describes the data and reuse without making a claim about a scientific finding.}
 Wire-cut striation marks can provide evidence for forensic source identification, but publicly available datasets and reproducible quantitative workflows for analyzing these marks are limited. We present 120 three-dimensional topographic scans in \texttt{x3p} format from aluminum wires cut with five KWS-105 wire cutters. The study includes four edges, three locations along each tool, and two replicates for every tool-edge-location combination. We provide scan metadata, manually extracted profiles, processed signals, pairwise cross-correlation values, images, and analysis code. The accompanying workflow covers scan inspection, profile and signal extraction, cross-correlation-based alignment, pairwise similarity visualization, and variability assessment across replicates, stagings, and acquisitions. Technical validation shows higher cross-correlations for same-source comparisons than for different-source comparisons and decreasing variability as scanning conditions become more consistent. The dataset and workflow support the development, evaluation, and reproducible comparison of quantitative methods for wire-cut evidence.

# Background \& Summary {#sec-background-summary .unnumbered}


In forensic analysis, marks left at crime scenes play an important role, and forensic examiners are particularly interested in identifying their origin, a process known as the Source Identification Problem in Forensic Science [@lindleyProblemForensicScience1977]. The forensic science community focuses on two distinct problems: the **specific source problem**, in which examiners aim to determine whether a mark was left by a particular tool, and the **common source problem**, in which examiners aim to determine whether two marks were left by the same tool. Currently, accepted practice for both problems relies on visual inspection of physical items under a comparison microscope. Examiners then report their conclusions according to the Theory of Identification [@afteAssociationFirearmTool1998], developed by the Association of Firearm and Toolmark Examiners (AFTE), using one of three categories: *identification*, in which the marks are believed to have been made by the same source; *elimination*, in which the marks are believed to have been made by different tools; and *inconclusive*, in which the similarities or dissimilarities between marks are insufficient to support either identification or elimination. This process has been criticized by the National Research Council (NRC) [@nationalresearchcouncilu.s.StrengtheningForensicScience2009a] and the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) [@presidentscouncilofadvisorsonscienceandtechnologyForensicScienceCriminal2016] for its lack of objectivity and absence of quantifiable measurements, such as error rates.

In discussing error rates, Biedermann [@biedermannStrangePersistenceSource2022] differentiates between internal and external perspectives. The external perspective allows general statements based on black-box studies that relate examiners' conclusions to ground truth; however, it does not consider the evidence in a particular case. Introducing an internal perspective requires a quantitative evaluation of the similarity of specific evidence and, in particular, objective algorithmic evaluations.


<!-- the data here comes out of the blue - needs more motivation
, which highlights the need for datasets with known ground truth for conclusion validation made through similarity comparison. -->


To train algorithms, we need data from scenarios with known ground truth. Because data collected at crime scenes are not suitable for this purpose, we used specific tools to cut wires under controlled conditions and collected the resulting marks for training. This approach enables comparisons between ground truth and the classification results produced by trained algorithms, with similarity quantified using error rates.

\agentreview{Clarify whether the error rates quantify similarity or the performance of the resulting classifications. The current sentence states that similarity itself is quantified using error rates.}


Advances in microscopy have made it possible to move from optical two-dimensional imaging to digital three-dimensional topographic scanning, allowing algorithmic assessment of the similarity between pairs of forensic pattern evidence [@bonfantiVisualisationConfocalMicroscopy2000]. This transition has already supported practical advances in bullet and cartridge comparisons, including visual inspection of bullet line scans from three-dimensional topographic images [@smithLinescanImagingBallistics2002], the use of features extracted by fast Fourier transform (FFT) as the basis of an artificial intelligence system [@liBallisticsProjectileImage2006], an automated pilot study based on consecutively matching striae [@chuPilotStudyAutomated2010] (a feature also used by some laboratories in casework), and the incorporation of three-dimensional imaging into routine casework at the Alabama Department of Forensic Sciences (ADFS) [@mcclarinAddingObjectiveComponent2015].

When cut wires are found at a crime scene, understanding the characteristics of marks left by bladed tools becomes essential. When a blade cuts a wire, it leaves striations on the surface, as shown in @fig-cut-microscope. These striations provide a basis for similarity assessment and source identification. Similar scans have supported the development of quantitative methods for analyzing firearms and other toolmark evidence. For example, studies of screwdriver striations have examined key factors affecting comparisons, including angles of attack [@baikerToolmarkVariabilityQuality2015a], rotational axes [@garciaInfluenceAxialRotation2017], and cutting directions [@cuellarAlgorithmForensicToolmark2024]. Foundational research on forensic toolmarks has also emphasized data collection and analysis, including the collection and distribution of datasets for bullet and toolmark analysis [@maNISTBulletSignature2004; @zhengNISTBallisticsToolmark2016], numerical methods for improving accuracy and consistency [@chuAutomaticIdentificationBullet2013; @vorburgerApplicationsCrosscorrelationFunctions2011], and techniques for quantifying similarity [@hareAutomaticMatchingBullet2017; @juOpenSourceImplementationCMPS2022].

Criminal convictions have relied on cut-wire evidence and related testimony. However, no public database supports assessment of (1) the similarity between striations on wires cut with the same tool or (2) error rates in source identification. Public wire-cut datasets are therefore urgently needed.

In this study, we provide a publicly available dataset of wire-cut scans, develop a systematic pipeline to analyze the data quantitatively, and introduce numerical measures for similarity assessment beyond visual inspection. The dataset includes multiple types of files, as summarized in @tbl-data-overview.

To ensure full reproducibility, we describe each step in detail, including how we collected and processed the wire-cut samples in Cutting wires, extracted profiles from the scanned wire cuts in Extract profiles, filtered signals from the profiles in Filtered signals, and aligned signals using the cross-correlation function (CCF) as a similarity measure in Align signals. Data Records describes where the dataset is hosted. Technical Validation evaluates the consistency of the assumptions and results and assesses variability. Usage Notes explains how to use the code for signal creation, alignment, analysis, validation, and visualization described in Methods and Technical Validation. Code Availability lists the code provided for reproducibility and future research. We anticipate that this dataset and analysis pipeline will support research on wire-cut evidence, including future studies of real-world crime-scene evidence.


# Methods {#sec-methods .unnumbered}


In this study, we used aluminum wire to create cuts. \hh{more details: thickness, brand?} The physical properties of aluminum wire make it an excellent material for retaining marks while remaining relatively easy to bend and nontoxic; \hh{i.e., with a hardness of XXX,} aluminum is soft enough for tools to leave marks but hard enough to resist damage when cut samples are handled under the microscope. In casework, aluminum wire is less common than lead or copper wire. We avoided using lead in the laboratory because of its toxicity. \hh{XXX look up the hardness value of aluminum, copper, and lead.}


## Cutting wires {#sec-cutting-wires .unnumbered}


We used 16-gauge, 1.5-mm anodized aluminum wire to create this wire-cut dataset. For each cut, a 4-inch piece was unspooled and cut with a model KWS-105 Kaiweets wire cutter at one of three blade locations (inner, middle, or outer) to produce one replicate, as shown in @fig-cut-tent-scan (a). Each piece was then cut in half to create 2-inch pieces for each pair of edges, AB and CD. A Sharpie line marked the cut ends, yielding four samples. We then followed the standard scanning protocol for the confocal microscope shown in @fig-cut-tent-scan (b) to scan the wire-tip surfaces. The surfaces were scanned at a resolution of $0.645 \mu m \times 0.645 \mu m$ per square pixel and saved in \texttt{x3p} format. @fig-cut-tent-scan (c) shows the AB and CD sides, with C on the reverse of A and D on the reverse of B. We separated the AB and CD sides into two pieces along the bend, resulting in eight scans. We repeated this process for all three blade locations and five wire cutters, with two replicates for each tool-edge-location combination, resulting in a sample of 120 scans. Each piece was labeled according to the following naming convention: T(ool) 1/2/3/4/5, (Edge) A/B/C/D, W(ire), L(ocation) I(nner)/M(iddle)/O(uter), and R(epetition) 1/2. For example, T1AW-LI-R1 denotes the first repetition of a piece cut by tool 1 on edge A at the inner location. To minimize errors in the sampling protocol, two team members cut and labeled the wires together. One team member then scanned the samples in a specified order and named the scans according to the naming convention, and a third team member checked the saved data.

## Extract profiles {#sec-extract-profiles .unnumbered}


Numerical comparisons between two replicates cannot be performed directly on the \texttt{x3p} files. We must first extract representative profiles from the scans. A profile is a sequence of surface-height values along a user-drawn line. After processing, this profile becomes a signal representing one scan and is used for subsequent comparisons. The profile captures most features of the scan and is drawn orthogonally to the striation marks, which are characterized by variations in groove height. We therefore draw a line across the scan region to capture as much striation information as possible, as shown in dark blue in @fig-T1AW-LI-R1-profiles-signals (a). We then examine the height values along this line. The resulting profile function is plotted in @fig-T1AW-LI-R1-profiles-signals (b) and must be processed before it becomes a useful signal.


## Filtered signals {#sec-filtered-signals .unnumbered}


After extracting the profile, we process it to obtain the signal. Two Gaussian filters, as discussed by Cleveland et al. [@clevelandLocalRegressionModels1992], are applied to each profile. First, we use a large low-pass filter with a bandwidth of 400 microns to remove the large-scale trend, which would otherwise overwhelm the signal. We then use a small high-pass filter with a bandwidth of 40 microns to average noise and remove spikes. Finally, we remove the extreme tail values and use the resulting signal for subsequent comparisons, as shown in @fig-T1AW-LI-R1-profiles-signals (c).

## Align signals {#sec-align-signals .unnumbered}


After extracting signals from different scans, we compare them by maximizing the CCF between each pair to determine their optimal numerical alignment. We compare all possible pairs; for example, the comparison between T1AW-LI-R1 and T1AW-LI-R2 corresponds to a row in @fig-scans-pair. We expect signals from two replicates with the same tool-edge-location combination, as shown in the first two columns of @fig-signals-pair-alignment, to be relatively similar. Their alignments should therefore show substantial overlap and yield high CCF values close to 1. The alignments and values in the rightmost column of @fig-signals-pair-alignment meet these expectations.

# Technical Validation {#sec-technical-validation .unnumbered}


We conducted technical validation in two areas: (1) signal processing and alignment and (2) variability assessment.


We validated scan processing and signal alignment as follows. We expected high CCF values between signals from the same source and low values between signals from different sources. @fig-signals-pair-alignment, shown earlier in Align signals, meets our expectation for same-source signals. As an example of a different-source comparison, we selected T1AW-LI-R1 and T2AW-LI-R1, shown in @fig-T1AW-LI-R1 and @fig-T2AW-LI-R1. Their signal alignment, shown in @fig-T1AW-LI-R1-T2AW-LI-R1, has a CCF value of 0.2, which is as low as expected. We also summarized the resulting CCFs for all pairwise comparisons in a boxplot and a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, shown in @fig-ccf-boxplot and @fig-ccf-ROC. The ROC curve plots sensitivity, or the true positive rate, against the false positive rate (FPR; 1 - specificity). The curve is close to the upper-left corner, indicating strong classification performance. A threshold of 0.589 controls the FPR below 0.05 with a false negative rate (FNR) of 0, whereas a threshold of 0.658 controls the FPR below 0.01 with an FNR of 0.02. \tom{(false positive rate (FPR) / false discovery rate (FDR) -> define the H0 or call it false identification rate (FIR)???)} These results are consistent with our expectations and validate our pipeline for processing and aligning signals.

The second validation assessed variability in the pipeline across replicates, stagings, and acquisitions. We selected scans from tool 2 at the middle location for this assessment. Replicate variability was assessed using two different cuts at the same edge and position, as illustrated by the comparison in @fig-signals-pair-alignment in Align signals. To assess staging variability, we rescanned replicate 2 under the confocal microscope and introduced the staging label S into the naming protocol. The S1 designation is omitted from labels, so R2 is equivalent to R2-S1. For all four edges of tool 2 at the middle location, we created three stagings (R2, R2-S2, and R2-S3), computed pairwise CCFs between stagings, and calculated their mean and standard deviation (SD).


Within each staging, we further examined the effect of different acquisitions by keeping the samples on the confocal microscope while varying the lighting conditions. We introduced A as the acquisition label. For edge A at staging 3, we performed four acquisitions and omitted the A1 designation from the first acquisition label, so R2-S3 is equivalent to R2-S3-A1. For the other three edges, we conducted two acquisitions at staging 3, denoted by R2-S3 and R2-S3-A2. We again computed pairwise CCFs between stagings and calculated their mean and standard deviation.

\agentreview{This paragraph describes acquisition variability, but its final sentence says that CCFs were computed between stagings. Confirm whether “stagings” should be “acquisitions.”}


With this setup, we expected CCF values to become more consistent from replicate to staging to acquisition as the scanning conditions became progressively more stable. Consequently, variability should decrease along this sequence. We also compared replicates, stagings, and acquisitions, expecting smaller differences between acquisitions and stagings than between stagings and replicates. We visualized the results as scatter plots in @fig-rep_staging_acquisition, which also shows intervals spanning two standard deviations. The higher orange bars indicate an increase in the mean, and the narrower intervals indicate a decrease in the standard deviation. The detailed numerical results, including means, standard deviations, and differences between means, are shown in Table \ref{tbl-CCF-replicate-staging-acquisition} and confirm our expectations.


Our variability assessment does not include variation in CCF values caused by differences in the manual extraction of profiles from scans. To support reproduction of the results reported here, we have included the extraction locations and values for each scan.

# Usage Notes {#sec-usage-notes .unnumbered}


The \texttt{R} package \texttt{x3ptools} [@hofmannX3ptoolsToolsWorking2018], available from \texttt{CRAN}, supports working with files in \texttt{x3p} format. Sample \texttt{R} scripts for converting \texttt{x3p} scans into signals and aligning those signals are available in the `assessment/code` folder of the \texttt{GitHub} repository [heike/wirecuts-data](https://github.com/heike/wirecuts-data), as described in @tbl-code-overview.


```{r}
#| echo: FALSE
#| label: tbl-code-overview
#| tbl-cap: Overview of available code.
#| results: asis

code_files <- c(
  "1-create_pngs_from_x3p.R",
  "2-create_profiles_from_x3p.R",
  "3-create-single-profile-file.R",
  "4-create_signals_from_profiles.R",
  "5-create-images.R",
  "6-align-pairwise.R",
  "7-all-comparison-results.R"
)

string <- tibble(
  group_type = c(rep("Inspect raw scans", 1), rep("Extract profiles", 2), rep("Derive signals", 1), rep("Align signals", 3)),
  code_type = paste0("`", code_files, "`"),
  Description = c("obtain images of `x3p`s in `scans/`", "manually extract profiles from each scan", "create meta profile information", "derive signals from each profile", "create images for pairwise alignment", "compute pairwise alignment CCF values", "visualize comparison results"),
  Section = c("Cutting wires", "Extract profiles", "Extract profiles", "Filtered signals", "Align signals", "Align signals", "Align signals")
) %>%
  gt(rowname_col = "code_type", groupname_col = "group_type") %>%
  tab_options(table.width = pct(95), table.font.size = px(14.67)) %>%
  cols_width(Description ~ pct(45), Section ~ pct(30), everything() ~ pct(55)) %>%
  fmt_markdown() %>%
  as_latex()

# column widths code - start
# Keep the three generated columns within the 95% table width.
dimexprs <- str_extract_all(pattern = "dimexpr 0.[0-9]+", string[1])[[1]]
replacement <- paste("dimexpr", c(0.43, 0.31, 0.21))
string[1] <- str_replace_all(
  string[1],
  pattern = "dimexpr 0.[0-9]+",
  replacement = "dimexpr FIX"
)
for (i in seq_along(dimexprs)) {
  string[1] <- str_replace(string[1], "dimexpr FIX", replacement[i])
}

# Allow long monospaced filenames to wrap without changing table font size.
for (code_file in code_files) {
  escaped_file <- str_replace_all(code_file, "_", "\\\\_")
  string[1] <- str_replace(
    string[1],
    fixed(paste0("\\texttt{", escaped_file, "}")),
    fixed(paste0("\\path{", code_file, "}"))
  )
}
# column widths code - end

# fixing cross-references - start
crossrefs <- str_extract_all(pattern = "hyperlink\\{[^ {]*\\}\\{.*\\}", string[1])[[1]]
# now replace every one of these cross references with the Latex call to autoref
crossrefs <- unique(crossrefs) # only needed once
# crossrefs <- crossrefs[nchar(crossrefs) > 1] # and only real references need to be dealt with
cross_latex <- crossrefs %>%
  str_replace("\\{", "[") %>%
  str_replace("\\}", "]") %>%
  str_replace("hyperlink", "\\\\hyperref")

string2 <- string[1]
for (i in seq_along(crossrefs)) {
  string2 <- str_replace_all(string2, crossrefs[i] %>%
    str_replace_all("\\{", "\\\\{") %>%
    str_replace_all("\\}", "\\\\}"), cross_latex[i])
}
string[1] <- string2
# fixing cross-references - end

string
```


We conducted pairwise comparisons and visualized some of the results in Align signals and Technical Validation. Here, we present additional analysis plots. When the CCF values are displayed in a tile map across tools, locations, and edge combinations, we expect only the diagonal to contain high values close to 1, shown in orange, because the diagonal represents same-source comparisons. We expect the rest of the matrix to contain low values close to 0, shown in gray. The pattern in @fig-ccf-tilemap is generally consistent with this expectation, except for a few cases involving edge D of tool 5. The density plot in @fig-ccf-density shows the distributions of CCF values for same-source and different-source comparisons. The overlap between the tails of these distributions provides a rough threshold for drawing conclusions.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("images/ccf_tilemap.png")
```

# Code Availability {#sec-code-availability .unnumbered}


We made available all code used to inspect raw scans, extract profiles, derive signals, align signals, and visualize the comparison results discussed in Methods and Technical Validation. The files are described in @tbl-code-overview. All results can be reproduced using the provided code.
